lesson.title: Actin in Action: Microfilaments and the Machinery of Cell Movement
lesson.summary: Microfilaments are thin, dynamic protein cables built from actin subunits that give cells their shape, drive amoeboid movement, and, paired with myosin, generate the force behind muscle contraction.
lesson.body:
Microfilaments are the thinnest of the three cytoskeletal filament types, measuring only about seven nanometers in diameter, and they are built entirely from a single protein called actin. Individual actin molecules, sometimes called globular actin or G-actin, polymerize into long chains that twist around one another to form a helical filament known as filamentous actin, or F-actin. Like the other components of the cytoskeleton, microfilaments are far from static, they are constantly being assembled and disassembled as the cell's needs change from moment to moment.

Actin itself is a protein, which means, at its most basic level, it is a chain of amino acids linked together by peptide bonds and folded into a specific three-dimensional shape that allows individual actin molecules to bind to one another end to end. This connection back to amino acids matters because it highlights something true of the entire cytoskeleton: these structural systems are not made of some exotic specialized material, they are built from the same twenty amino acids used to construct every other protein in the cell, simply folded and assembled in a way that produces a strong, flexible, self-assembling filament rather than an enzyme or a membrane channel.

Microfilaments have a defined structural polarity, meaning the two ends of the filament are chemically different from one another. One end, called the plus end or barbed end, tends to add new actin subunits more quickly, while the other end, called the minus end or pointed end, tends to lose subunits more readily. Under the right cellular conditions, a filament can add subunits at the plus end at roughly the same rate it loses them at the minus end, a phenomenon called treadmilling, which allows the filament to maintain a constant length while effectively moving along its own length like a conveyor belt.

This dynamic assembly and disassembly is what makes microfilaments so useful for cell movement. Many cells, including certain white blood cells and single-celled amoebas, move by extending thin, sheet-like projections of their plasma membrane called lamellipodia or finger-like projections called pseudopodia, both of which are pushed outward by the rapid polymerization of actin filaments just beneath the membrane. As new actin subunits are added at the leading edge, they physically shove the membrane forward, and the rest of the cell body then follows. Microfilaments also form the structural core of microvilli, the tiny finger-like projections that dramatically increase the surface area of intestinal epithelial cells for nutrient absorption.

Beyond cell movement, microfilaments team up with a motor protein called myosin to generate contractile force, most famously inside muscle cells, where organized arrays of actin and myosin filaments slide past one another to shorten the muscle, but also in non-muscle cells, where a contractile ring made of actin and myosin pinches a dividing cell into two daughter cells during cytokinesis. Because microfilaments connect this directly back to the broader cytoskeleton, they represent one concrete example of how a single filament type, built from one relatively simple protein, can support functions as different as cell crawling, nutrient absorption, muscle contraction, and cell division, depending entirely on how the cell organizes and regulates it.
